patterns.title: Head and Shoulders Pattern — How to Read It | Market Credo
patterns.metaDescription: Learn to read the head and shoulders chart pattern — the two shoulders, the head and the neckline — an educational guide from Market Credo, Bhopal.
patterns.intro: The head and shoulders is a reversal structure made of three peaks — a higher middle peak (the head) between two lower, roughly equal peaks (the shoulders) — resting on a line called the neckline. It is studied as a sign that an existing uptrend may be losing strength.

sections.html:
Read left to right, the shape has three pushes higher. The first push forms the left shoulder. Price pulls back, then rises to a higher point — the head — before pulling back again. A third push rises to about the height of the first, forming the right shoulder. The two pullback lows in between define the neckline.

The pattern matters because the second lower peak (the right shoulder) shows buyers were unable to push price back to the previous high. That loss of momentum is the whole idea — the structure is a picture of a trend running out of fuel.

sections.h2: The neckline is the key line
sections.html:
Draw the neckline by connecting the two pullback lows either side of the head. Until price closes clearly beyond that line, the shape is only a possibility — an outline, not a confirmed pattern. Most readers treat a decisive close beyond the neckline as the point where the structure is confirmed.

  • A neckline can be flat, rising or falling — the angle is part of what you read.
  • After a break, price sometimes comes back to the neckline from the other side (a throwback) before continuing. That retest is a common place to study the pattern's behaviour.

sections.h2: Volume and the story it tells
sections.html: Volume often eases as the pattern develops — frequently lighter under the right shoulder than under the head. That fading participation is consistent with the idea of a weakening trend. Volume is context, not proof: read it alongside the structure rather than on its own.

sections.h2: The measured move, as a concept
sections.html: Students often ask how far a move might carry after a neckline break. As an educational concept, the vertical distance from the head to the neckline can be projected from the break point to give a sense of scale. Treat this as a way to understand proportion in the pattern — not as a forecast, and never as advice to act.

Flip the pattern upside down and it forms at the end of a downtrend instead: a lower middle trough (the head) between two shallower troughs (the shoulders), under a neckline. It is studied as the mirror image — a downtrend that may be losing strength.

• Forcing the shape. Not every three-peak wiggle is a head and shoulders. The shoulders should be roughly symmetrical and the head clearly higher.
  • Ignoring the neckline. An unbroken neckline means the pattern is unconfirmed. The outline alone is not enough.
  • Reading it in isolation. The pattern is one piece of structure. Weigh it against the wider trend, support and resistance, and overall context.

sections.h2: How we teach it at Market Credo
sections.html: In the classroom we teach the head and shoulders from first principles — why the structure forms, what the neckline represents, and how to confirm it — so you can recognise it on any chart yourself. The aim is an independent reader of price, not someone who depends on ready-made trades.

faqs.q: Is the head and shoulders a bullish or bearish pattern?
faqs.a: The classic head and shoulders forms at the end of an uptrend and is studied as a potential reversal lower. Its mirror image, the inverse head and shoulders, forms at the end of a downtrend and is studied as a potential reversal higher. Neither outcome is a certainty — it is one piece of structure to weigh with the rest of the chart.

faqs.q: How do I confirm a head and shoulders pattern?
faqs.a: Most readers wait for a decisive close beyond the neckline before treating the pattern as confirmed. A neckline that has not broken means the shape is still just an outline. At Market Credo we teach confirmation and context rather than acting on the outline alone.

related.note: the two-peak relative: two tops at roughly the same height instead of three peaks with a higher middle one, resting on the same kind of neckline and read the same way once the line breaks.

patterns.title: Double Top Pattern — How to Read It | Market Credo
patterns.metaDescription: Learn to read the double top chart pattern — the two peaks, the neckline and what confirms a break — an educational guide from Market Credo, Bhopal.
patterns.intro: A double top is a reversal structure made of two peaks at roughly the same height, separated by a pullback, with a line called the neckline drawn along the low between them. It is studied as a sign that an existing uptrend may be losing strength.

sections.html:
Read left to right, price advances and stalls at a first peak, pulls back to a low that holds, then advances a second time into roughly the same zone and stalls again. The two peaks are the tops; the line drawn along the pullback low between them is the neckline.

The structure matters because the second push could not better the first — it is a picture of a trend that has stopped making progress. Roughly equal is the operative phrase: the two tops rarely match exactly, and a modest overshoot or undershoot on the second is normal. What you are reading is a failure to extend, not a measurement to the tick.

An uptrend has to be in place first — without a prior advance there is nothing to reverse.

  • The advance stalls and forms the first top.
  • Price pulls back to a level that holds; that low defines the neckline.
  • A second advance retests the area of the first top and stalls in the same zone, forming the second top.
  • The structure is complete only when price closes decisively beyond the neckline. Until then it is an outline, not a pattern.

Time matters as much as shape. The two tops normally separate by a meaningful number of sessions; two peaks a couple of bars apart are noise, not structure.

sections.h2: The psychology behind the two tops
sections.html:
The first top is where an advance meets enough supply to halt it. The pullback brings in buyers who still read the trend as intact, and the second advance is their attempt to carry it further. When that attempt stalls in the same zone, it tells you the buyers driving the trend could not absorb what was waiting for them there.

There is a second group in the picture: traders who bought into the first top and have been holding a loss since. Near the second top they are close to breakeven, and some of them take that exit — which adds to supply exactly where the advance is already struggling.

The neckline is where these groups meet. It has held once, everyone can see it, and a decisive close beyond it removes the level the structure was resting on. Volume often eases on the second top compared with the first, which is consistent with fading participation — read it as context, not proof.

sections.h2: Validation rules — when the shape counts
sections.html:
Treat the shape as a pattern only when all of this is present:

  • A prior uptrend to reverse.
  • Two peaks in roughly the same zone, with neither dramatically higher.
  • A genuine reaction between them, not a shallow pause.
  • Visible separation in time between the two tops.
  • A neckline you can draw cleanly along the pullback low.
  • A decisive close beyond that neckline — a wick through the line, on its own, is not the same thing.

Miss any of these and what you have is a possibility, not a pattern.

sections.h2: Where the structure is confirmed, and where it stops being valid
sections.html:
Confirmation is conventionally taken as a decisive close beyond the neckline. Some readers wait for price to come back to the line from the other side — a throwback — before treating the break as settled, and that retest is a useful place to study how the structure behaves.

The reading is invalidated when price recovers above the higher of the two tops: the failure to extend that defined the pattern no longer holds, so the structure is gone. Between the neckline and the tops it is simply unresolved — neither confirmed nor invalid.

On scale, the vertical distance from the tops down to the neckline, projected from the break point, is taught as a way to understand the pattern's proportions. That is a concept for reading structure, not a forecast. We teach where a reading stops being valid; we do not tell anyone what to buy or sell, and nothing here is a recommendation.

• The break that does not hold. Price closes beyond the neckline and then recovers back inside the structure.
  • Forcing the shape. Any two bumps on a chart are not a double top.
  • A second peak far above or below the first. That is a different structure being read as this one.
  • No context. Reading the pattern without the wider trend, or without a second timeframe.
  • Treating the measured move as a promise rather than a way of thinking about scale.

sections.html: In the classroom we teach the double top from first principles — why the structure forms, what the neckline represents, how it is confirmed and when it is no longer valid — so you can read it on any chart yourself. The aim is an independent reader of price, not someone who depends on ready-made trades.

faqs.q: Is a double top a bullish or bearish pattern?
faqs.a: A double top forms after an uptrend and is studied as a potential reversal lower. Its mirror image, the double bottom, forms at the end of a downtrend and is studied as a potential reversal higher. Neither outcome is a certainty — it is one piece of structure to weigh with the rest of the chart.

faqs.q: How equal do the two tops have to be?
faqs.a: They should form in the same zone rather than match tick for tick. A modest overshoot or undershoot on the second attempt is normal. What matters is the failure to extend, and a neckline you can draw cleanly along the low between the two peaks.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a double top and a head and shoulders?
faqs.a: A double top has two peaks of similar height; a head and shoulders has three, with a higher middle peak between two lower ones. Both rest on a neckline, and both are read the same way once that line breaks decisively.

related.note: the near neighbour: three peaks with a higher middle one instead of two tops of equal height, resting on the same kind of neckline and read the same way once the line breaks.
